title: Conservation of Mass
seo_title: Grade 5 Conservation of Mass Worksheets: Heating, Cooling, Mixing and Graphs
standard_text: Measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling, or mixing substances, the total weight of matter is conserved.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on conservation of mass (NGSS 5-PS1-2): mass before and after melting, freezing, dissolving and chemical changes, sealed vs open containers, and bar graphs. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: In any change, the total mass stays the same.
key_sub: Heating, cooling, mixing and chemical changes rearrange particles but never destroy them. If the mass goes down, something escaped.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter is made of particles. In any change, the particles are rearranged, but none are created or destroyed. So the total mass stays the same. This is called conservation of mass.

It is true when matter is heated or cooled (melting, freezing, boiling), when it is mixed or dissolved, and even in chemical changes that make new substances.

If the mass seems to go down, something escaped, usually a gas or water vapor from an open container.

Example

40 g of salt is dissolved in 300 g of water. What is the mass of the salt water?

The salt is still there as tiny particles.

300 + 40 = 340.

Answer: 340 g

Example

In an open cup, an antacid fizzes in water. The mass goes from 210 g to 204 g. Was matter destroyed?

210 − 204 = 6 g.

A gas escaped into the air.

Answer: No. 6 g of gas left the cup.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking ice is heavier than the same water. It takes up more space but has the same mass.
  • Thinking a gas has no mass. When a gas escapes, the container gets lighter.
  • Thinking a dissolved solid adds no mass. Its mass is still there.
  • Testing a chemical change in an open cup and deciding matter was destroyed. Use a sealed container.

faq.q: What is the law of conservation of mass?
faq.a: Matter cannot be created or destroyed. In any change, the total mass before equals the total mass after, as long as nothing gets in or out.

faq.q: Does ice weigh more than water?
faq.a: No. Ice takes up a little more space, but the same water has the same mass as a solid or a liquid.

faq.q: Why does the mass go down when baking soda and vinegar fizz in an open cup?
faq.a: The reaction makes carbon dioxide gas, which escapes into the air. In a sealed bag the mass stays the same.

faq.q: Is mass conserved in chemical changes?
faq.a: Yes. The particles rearrange into new substances, but the total mass stays the same.

items.q: Maya burns a piece of steel wool in a closed jar. The mass of the jar stays the same. Why?
c: The new substances stayed inside the closed jar.
The jar absorbed the extra mass.
items.e: Burning made new substances, but nothing could escape from the closed jar.

items.q: The graph shows the mass of a cup before and after mixing yeast and hydrogen peroxide. Was the cup most likely sealed or open?
c: sealed, because the mass did not change
open, because the mass went up
sealed, because the mass went down
open, because gas escaped and the mass went down
items.e: The mass dropped from 65 g to 55 g. A gas from the change escaped, so the cup was open.

items.q: Why must all the parts be weighed together, like the bag, the cup and both substances?
c: to measure the total mass of everything that was there before and after
because a scale cannot weigh one thing
items.e: The total mass of all the matter is what stays the same.
